title: Cloud Application Integration
summary: Software as a service platforms commonly extend themselves through OAuth integrations, where a user consents to let an application read mailbox, file or directory data on their behalf. This technique abuses that model for persistence. The actor can register a new application, add an existing third-party application to the tenant, or take over an integration that already exists. Consent is granted by an attacker-controlled account that holds high privilege, and the resulting access survives the loss of that account in many cases, because the credential belongs to the application and not to the user. In Microsoft 365 an application gains access through an application object with a service principal and assigned application permissions or roles, which means it can act without a signed-in person and therefore without multi-factor authentication prompts. The result is durable, API-based collection and automated exfiltration over time. Detection leans on the directory and audit trail rather than on endpoint data: new application registrations, new service principals, admin consent grants, credential additions to existing applications, and sign-ins from a service principal with no interactive user. The differentiator from normal business is governance: sanctioned integrations have an owner, a ticket and a business purpose, while malicious ones often appear with a newly created or unlicensed privileged granting account.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker keeps access to a cloud service using an application integration, not a user login. Cloud platforms let apps ask for permission to read your mail and files. If an attacker controls such an app, or takes one over, that permission keeps working. It keeps working even after the original user is locked out. The attacker then reads data through the app, quietly and for a long time.
beginner.whyItMatters: A normal password reset or account lockout does not remove an application permission. Teams can therefore believe an incident is closed while access remains. Apps also act without a person present, which means the usual multi-factor approval never appears. This gives an attacker a long, silent path to mail, files and directory data. It also gives them a way to copy that data out automatically. Many organisations never review which apps hold consent, so the access can live on for months.
howItWorks: The attacker gains a privileged cloud account, often through phishing or password spraying.
They register a new application in the cloud directory, or they take over an integration that already exists.
They grant that application permission to read mail, files or user details, sometimes using an admin consent screen.
The platform then issues the application its own credential, called a token, that works without a human login.
Because the access belongs to the app, disabling the original user account does not always end it.
The attacker uses the app to read and copy out data over a long period, hidden among normal API traffic.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where you give a delivery firm a permanent key to your hallway for parcels. Later you fall out with the person who arranged that key, and you change your own locks. The delivery company still has its key, and it can still walk in whenever it likes. Nobody questions it, because a delivery van at the door looks completely normal.
takeaways: Application permissions can outlive the user account that granted them.
Review which third-party apps hold consent, and who approved each one.
Alert on new applications, new consent grants and app sign-ins without a user.

objectives: Explain how OAuth consent gives an application standing access to cloud data.
Describe why disabling a user account may not remove an application's access.
Explain why application tokens bypass interactive multi-factor authentication.
Locate the audit events that record app registration, consent and credential changes.
Compare a sanctioned integration with an attacker-created one using ownership and purpose.
